title: Variable Scope
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of variable scope and identify when it is appropriate in a Java program.
Apply at least one of the lesson topics—local variables—in a small, readable example.
Predict the example result and check it against the stated output or a boundary-case test.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study variable scope with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you choose types and variable scope deliberately instead of relying on guesses about values. In this lesson, focus on local variables and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: A variable has a declared type and a scope. Initialize local variables before reading them; fields have defined default values, but relying on defaults can hide missing business logic. The important habit is to make the assumptions explicit and use the code example as a small experiment.

content_blocks.title: How the pieces fit
content_blocks.text: Connect local variables with parameters before choosing an implementation. The example is a small, observable case; extend it by changing one input and checking a boundary, invalid value, or compatibility limit where relevant.

items.title: Local variables
items.text: A variable has a declared type and a scope. Initialize local variables before reading them; fields have defined default values, but relying on defaults can hide missing business logic.

items.title: Parameters
items.text: A method gives a named contract to a unit of behavior. Keep responsibilities focused, define clear parameter and return types, and test typical, boundary, and invalid cases independently.

items.title: Instance fields
items.text: Java variables have declared or inferred static types and a defined scope. Local `var` infers a compile-time type from the initializer; it does not make the language dynamically typed. Apply that reasoning specifically to instance fields and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test.

items.title: Static fields
items.text: A class defines state and behavior; an object is an instance. Encapsulation protects invariants by keeping mutable state private and validating updates through a small public API.

items.title: Block scope
items.text: Concurrency introduces shared-state ordering and cancellation concerns. Prefer task abstractions and immutable data where possible, coordinate access explicitly, and always define shutdown, timeout, and failure behavior.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Keep one clear hypothesis per experiment. Check the version, read the error message, test boundaries, and record what evidence supports your conclusion.

common_mistakes.problem: Applying the rule from memory without checking its exact contract.
common_mistakes.why: Small differences in type, scope, API version, or input shape can change the result.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the relevant official API/language documentation and build a minimal reproducer.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing only a single happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Boundary values and failures often reveal assumptions hidden by the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add an empty, boundary, or invalid case and state the expected behavior before running it.

common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify the actual cause of a different result.
common_mistakes.fix: Change one factor at a time and keep a short record of observed behavior.
